title: Québécois French
goal: Understand everyday Québec French: recognize its key informal words and expressions, its main pronunciation features, and the question particle -tu, and know which forms to use yourself.

items.fr: Tu viens-tu ? → Est-ce que tu viens ?
items.en: recognizing informal Québec forms and their standard equivalents

drills.explain: In informal Québec speech, [[-tu]] after the verb marks a yes/no question. It's not the pronoun [[tu]]: [[Ça marche-tu ?]] = Does it work?

drills.text: J'ai de la misère ___ comprendre mon voisin.
drills.en: I have a hard time understanding my neighbour.
drills.explain: [[avoir de la misère à]] + infinitive = to have trouble doing something (informal Québec).

drills.prompt: Your colleague says “Je suis tanné de l'hiver.” How does he feel?
drills.explain: [[être tanné de]] = to be fed up with (informal Québec). In France: [[en avoir marre de]].

example.fr: Mon char est encore au garage.
example.en: My car is at the garage again.

items.note: Standard Québec French: [[une auto]] or [[une voiture]]. In France, [[un char]] is a tank or a parade float!

example.fr: Je te présente ma blonde, Sofia.
example.en: Let me introduce my girlfriend, Sofia.

items.note: Whatever her hair colour! In France: [[ma copine]].

example.fr: Mon chum vient nous rejoindre pour souper.
example.en: My boyfriend is joining us for supper.

items.note: Pronounced like [[tchomme]]. [[mes chums]] can also mean my buddies, and [[ma chum]] my (female) friend.
Standard in Québec, even in ads and newspapers. France says [[faire les magasins]] or [[faire du shopping]].

example.fr: Je passe au dépanneur acheter du lait.
example.en: I'm stopping at the corner store to buy milk.

items.note: Often shortened to [[le dep]]. In France, [[un dépanneur]] is a tow-truck driver or repairman.

items.en: to have a hard time doing (Québec)

example.fr: J'ai de la misère à me lever le matin.
example.en: I have a hard time getting up in the morning.

items.note: Pronounced [[platte]], with a clear t. [[C'est plate que tu partes]] = it's too bad you're leaving (subjunctive after an emotion!).

example.en: I didn't like it at all.

items.note: Like [[tout à l'heure]]: the tense tells you if it's past or future. [[Tantôt, j'ai vu Karim]] = earlier.

steps.title: A Saturday plan in Montréal
steps.intro: Québec French is a full, living variety of French, spoken by about seven million people. In the news, at school and at work, it's close to the French you've learned, with a different accent. With friends, it becomes much more informal, just as Parisian French does. Listen first, then read.

blocks.title: Tu viens-tu magasiner ?
blocks.context: Camille, from Montréal, calls her colleague Karim, who arrived from Morocco a year ago. They're friends, so the register is very informal.

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Salut Karim ! Tu viens-tu magasiner avec moi samedi ?
lines.en: Hi Karim! Do you want to come shopping with me on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Karim
lines.fr: Oui, pourquoi pas ! On prend ton char ?
lines.en: Yes, why not! Are we taking your car?

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Ben non, il est encore au garage. Je suis tannée, il est toujours brisé ! On va prendre le métro.
lines.en: Well no, it's at the garage again. I'm fed up, it's always broken! We'll take the metro.

lines.speaker: Karim
lines.fr: C'est correct. Ton chum vient avec nous ?
lines.en: That's fine. Is your boyfriend coming with us?

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Non, Maxime travaille. Il a de la misère à avoir des fins de semaine de congé, ces temps-ci.
lines.en: No, Maxime's working. He has a hard time getting weekends off these days.

lines.speaker: Karim
lines.en: Oh, that's too bad for him.

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Ouin. Mais il va nous rejoindre pour souper. Avant de partir, il faut que j'arrête au dépanneur.
lines.en: Yeah. But he'll join us for supper. Before we leave, I have to stop at the corner store.

lines.speaker: Karim
lines.fr: Pis tantôt, tu m'as dit qu'il allait neiger samedi ?
lines.en: And earlier, you told me it was going to snow on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Camille
lines.fr: Non, pantoute ! J'ai dit qu'il allait faire frette. Mets ta tuque !
lines.en: No, not at all! I said it was going to be freezing. Wear your toque!

blocks.title: A voicemail from Camille
blocks.context: Saturday morning, Camille leaves Karim a message.
blocks.fr: Allô Karim, c'est Camille. Écoute, petit changement : mon chum a fini plus tôt, fait que finalement, on va magasiner tous les trois. On se rejoint au métro Berri à une heure, c'est-tu correct pour toi ? Pis apporte un sac, je pense qu'il y a des soldes au centre-ville. Rappelle-moi tantôt. Bye !
blocks.en: Hi Karim, it's Camille. Listen, small change: my boyfriend finished earlier, so in the end the three of us are going shopping. We'll meet at Berri metro station at one o'clock, is that OK for you? And bring a bag, I think there are sales downtown. Call me back later. Bye!

options: Camille's boyfriend is coming shopping too
blocks.explain: [[mon chum a fini plus tôt, fait que finalement, on va magasiner tous les trois]]: [[fait que]] = so; [[tous les trois]] = the three of us.

blocks.prompt: In “Rappelle-moi tantôt”, when should Karim call?
blocks.explain: With an imperative or future, [[tantôt]] means later today, like [[tout à l'heure]].

blocks.title: Pronunciation tendencies
blocks.body:
You don't need to imitate the accent, but recognizing these features makes Québec speech much easier to follow:

- **t and d before i and u become [ts] and [dz]**: [[tu dis]] sounds like *tsu dzi*, [[petit]] like *p'tsi*, [[mardi]] like *mar-dzi*. This is the most typical feature, and it's very widespread in Québec French, including on the news.
- **Short i, u, ou in closed syllables sound more open**: [[vite]], [[musique]], [[toute]] have a relaxed vowel, closer to English *bit*, *put*.
- **Long vowels can glide** (in relaxed speech): [[père]], [[fête]] may sound like *paère*, *faète*.
- **[[â]] and [[a]] are distinct**: [[pâte]] (pasta) has a deep, back vowel; [[patte]] (paw) a front one.
- **[[moé]], [[toé]]** for [[moi]], [[toi]] (and [[frette]] for [[froid]]): an older pronunciation, heard today mostly in very informal speech. It isn't a Québec invention: a similar *oé* pronunciation seems to have been common in France too, centuries ago, before the modern *oi* [wa] won out there.
- **The question particle [[-tu]]**: [[Tu viens-tu ?]] [[C'est-tu correct ?]] = yes/no question, informal.

blocks.title: Myths and facts
blocks.body:
- **Myth: “Québec French is old French.”** Some features come from the regional French of 17th- and 18th-century settlers, but Québec French has evolved for four centuries, like every language. It has its own modern standard, used by Radio-Canada, universities and the government.
- **Myth: “People from France can't understand Québécois.”** Formal Québec French is understood everywhere. Very informal speech, full of local words and a fast rhythm, can surprise a European ear, just as Marseille slang can surprise a Montrealer.
- **Fact: Québec protects French actively.** The OQLF proposes French terms instead of English ones: [[courriel]], [[clavarder]] (to chat online), [[balado]] (podcast). Ironically, everyday French in France often uses the English words ([[mail]], [[podcast]]).
- **Fact: anglicisms exist in informal speech** ([[c'est le fun]], [[checker]], [[une job]]), because of contact with English. Many Québécois use them at home and avoid them at work.
- **[[le joual]]** (from a local pronunciation of [[cheval]]) is the name given to the urban working-class speech of Montréal. Literature made it famous, especially Michel Tremblay's plays, starting with *Les Belles-sœurs* (1968), which brought it to the stage and made it a symbol of Québec identity. Today the word is often used more loosely for very informal Québec French.
- **Swear words** ([[sacres]]) come from church vocabulary. You'll hear them in films and on the street: recognize them, don't use them.

blocks.title: Using Québec words wisely
blocks.body:
- **Register mismatch**: [[Je suis tanné de votre dossier]] to a government officer ✗. With officials and at work, use standard French ([[Je suis découragé par ces délais]]).
- **Imitating the accent on purpose**: it can sound like mockery. Speak your French naturally; Québécois appreciate the effort, not the imitation.
- **False friends with France**: in Québec, [[le dîner]] is lunch; in France, it's dinner. Check the time of an invitation!
- **[[blonde]] and [[chum]] are not about hair or casual friendship only**: [[C'est mon chum]] said by a woman usually means *my boyfriend*.
- **Thinking it's “bad French”**: these are regional and informal forms, not mistakes. Every francophone country has its own.

blocks.title: Beyond Québec
blocks.body: Canada has other French varieties too. **Acadian French** (New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, PEI) has its own words and accent; in southeast New Brunswick, **chiac** mixes French and English. **Franco-Ontarian** and **Franco-Manitoban** French are close to Québec French, with local features. At work in Canada, you'll hear all of them, plus the French of Haiti, Africa, the Maghreb and Europe.

steps.title: Tune your ear
steps.intro: Depending on your device, the voice may have a European or a Canadian accent. The pronunciation tips describe what you'll hear from Québec speakers.

blocks.title: Listen and repeat
blocks.note: Repeat in your own accent. The goal is to recognize, not to imitate.

lines.en: Are you coming shopping on Saturday?
lines.tip: The second [[tu]] is a question particle, not a pronoun.

lines.en: I'm stopping at the corner store.

lines.fr: J'ai de la misère à me lever le matin.
lines.en: I have a hard time getting up in the morning.

lines.fr: C'est plate, il pleut toute la fin de semaine.
lines.en: Too bad, it's raining all weekend.

blocks.fr: Je suis tanné de chercher un stationnement. Demain, je laisse mon char à la maison pis je prends l'autobus.
blocks.en: I'm fed up with looking for parking. Tomorrow, I'm leaving my car at home and taking the bus.
blocks.prompt: What will the speaker do tomorrow?
options: Take the bus instead of the car
blocks.explain: [[je laisse mon char à la maison pis je prends l'autobus]]: [[char]] = car, [[pis]] = and.

blocks.fr: Le film ? Non, j'ai pas aimé ça pantoute. C'était long pis plate.
blocks.en: The movie? No, I didn't like it at all. It was long and boring.
blocks.prompt: What did the speaker think of the movie?
options: She didn't like it at all: long and boring

blocks.fr: Ma blonde pis moi, on a de la misère à trouver un appartement. Tout est trop cher présentement.
blocks.en: My girlfriend and I are having a hard time finding an apartment. Everything is too expensive right now.
options: He and his girlfriend can't easily find an affordable apartment
blocks.explain: [[avoir de la misère à trouver]] = to have trouble finding; [[présentement]] = currently.

blocks.fr: Je t'appelle tantôt, après le souper.
blocks.explain: [[tantôt]] = later today; [[le souper]] = dinner in Québec.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.intro: Recognition first, then translation into standard French.

blocks.prompt: Match the Québec word with its standard equivalent.

blocks.fr: Bienvenue ! Pis si t'as besoin d'autre chose, gêne-toi pas.
blocks.en: You're welcome! And if you need anything else, don't be shy.
options: You're welcome, and don't hesitate to ask for more
blocks.explain: After [[merci]], Québécois often answer [[Bienvenue !]] = You're welcome. [[Gêne-toi pas]] = don't be shy, don't hesitate.

blocks.prompt: A Québécoise friend invites you “pour dîner, samedi”. When should you come?
Rewrite in standard French: “Mon char est brisé, j'ai de la misère à aller travailler.”
accept: Ma voiture est en panne, j'ai du mal à aller travailler.
Mon auto est en panne, j'ai du mal à aller travailler.
Ma voiture est en panne, j'ai de la difficulté à aller travailler.
Mon auto est en panne, j'ai de la difficulté à aller travailler.
Ma voiture est brisée, j'ai du mal à aller travailler.
Mon auto est brisée, j'ai du mal à aller travailler.
Ma voiture est en panne, j'ai des difficultés à aller travailler.
blocks.explain: [[char]] → [[voiture]] or [[auto]] (feminine!); [[avoir de la misère à]] → [[avoir du mal à]]. [[brisé]] (broken) is common in Québec; [[en panne]] is standard everywhere for a car.

blocks.text: C'est plate que tu ___ demain. Tu reviens-___ bientôt ?
blocks.en: It's too bad you're leaving tomorrow. Are you coming back soon?
blocks.explain: [[c'est plate que]] expresses a feeling, so subjunctive [[partes]] (Unit 06). [[-tu]] is the informal question particle.

blocks.fr: Tantôt, j'ai croisé ton chum au dépanneur. Il m'a dit que vous partiez en Gaspésie la fin de semaine prochaine.
blocks.en: Earlier, I ran into your boyfriend at the corner store. He told me you're going to the Gaspé next weekend.
blocks.prompt: When did the speaker see the boyfriend?
Which word would be fine in a formal email to a Québec employer?
blocks.explain: [[la fin de semaine]] is standard Québec French. The other three are informal.

blocks.prompt: Rewrite in standard French: “Je suis tanné, le film était plate.”
accept: J'en ai assez, le film était ennuyeux.
J'en ai marre, le film était ennuyeux.
J'en ai assez, le film était ennuyant.
J'en ai marre, le film était ennuyant.
J'en ai assez, le film était nul.
J'en ai marre, le film était nul.
blocks.explain: [[être tanné]] → [[en avoir assez / marre]]; [[plate]] → [[ennuyeux]] ([[ennuyant]] is common in Québec).

blocks.fr: Je passe au dépanneur, tu veux-tu quelque chose ?
blocks.explain: [[-tu]] after the verb marks an informal yes/no question. Write what you hear here, but in your own writing use [[Est-ce que tu veux…]] or [[Tu veux… ?]].

blocks.prompt: A Québécois friend sends you this text: “Salut ! Chus tanné de rester chez nous. Tu viens-tu magasiner à soir ? Mon char est au garage, fait qu'on prendrait le métro. Ma blonde vient aussi. Pis après, on pourrait souper au resto. Réponds-moi tantôt !” First, rewrite it in standard French. Then write your reply (in standard French, friendly register).
blocks.promptFr: Réécrivez le texto en français standard, puis répondez.
checklist: Every Québec form turned into standard French (chus, à soir, char, fait que, blonde, pis, tantôt)
The question particle -tu turned into a normal question
A friendly reply that accepts or declines
A reason with a precise connector

models.label: Model answer
models.fr:
En français standard : « Salut ! J'en ai assez de rester à la maison. Est-ce que tu veux faire les magasins ce soir ? Ma voiture est au garage, donc on prendrait le métro. Ma copine vient aussi. Et après, on pourrait dîner au restaurant. Réponds-moi tout à l'heure ! »

Ma réponse : Salut ! Bonne idée, je viens avec plaisir. Par contre, je finis le travail à 18 h, donc je ne pourrai pas être là avant 18 h 30. On se retrouve à la station Berri ? Pour le resto, je suis partant. À tantôt !
models.en:
In standard French: “Hi! I'm fed up with staying home. Do you want to go shopping tonight? My car's at the garage, so we'd take the metro. My girlfriend's coming too. And afterwards, we could have dinner at a restaurant. Answer me later!”

My reply: Hi! Good idea, I'd love to come. However, I finish work at 6 p.m., so I won't be able to be there before 6:30. Shall we meet at Berri station? For the restaurant, I'm in. See you later!

blocks.prompt: A friend who just arrived in Montréal asks you: “What Québec words should I know?” Explain five words or expressions, with an example and the standard equivalent for each, and give one piece of advice about when to use them.
checklist: Five words with meaning and standard equivalent
An example sentence for at least three
Advice on register (with friends vs at work)

models.label: Model answer
models.fr: D'abord, « magasiner », c'est-à-dire faire les magasins : on dit ça partout au Québec, même à la télé. Ensuite, « le dépanneur », c'est la petite épicerie du coin. Attention aux repas : le dîner, c'est à midi, et le souper, c'est le soir. Avec tes amis, tu vas entendre « je suis tanné », autrement dit « j'en ai assez », et « c'est plate », qui veut dire que c'est ennuyeux ou dommage. Enfin, « pantoute », ça veut dire pas du tout. Mon conseil : comprends tout, mais au travail, utilise surtout « magasiner », « dépanneur » et « fin de semaine ». Les autres, garde-les pour tes amis.
models.en: First, “magasiner”, that is, going shopping: people say it everywhere in Québec, even on TV. Next, “le dépanneur” is the little corner store. Careful with meals: “le dîner” is at noon, and “le souper” is in the evening. With your friends, you'll hear “je suis tanné”, in other words “I'm fed up”, and “c'est plate”, which means it's boring or too bad. Finally, “pantoute” means not at all. My advice: understand everything, but at work, mostly use “magasiner”, “dépanneur” and “fin de semaine”. Keep the others for your friends.

summary:
- Recognize key Québec words: [[char]], [[blonde]], [[chum]], [[magasiner]], [[dépanneur]], [[être tanné]], [[avoir de la misère à]], [[c'est plate]], [[pantoute]], [[tantôt]]
- Hear typical features: [[tu dis]] as *tsu dzi*, open vowels, the question particle [[-tu]]
- Translate informal Québec speech into standard French, and avoid the [[dîner]] / [[souper]] trap
- Use Québec standard words ([[magasiner]], [[fin de semaine]]) anywhere, informal ones only with friends

meta.notes: Affrication now "very widespread"; moé/toé presented as an older pronunciation with hedging; joual described respectfully (Michel Tremblay, Les Belles-sœurs). Removed non-homophone dictation accepts.
